utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody now in the third courtroom, which is Courtroom I. Before we ask the witness to be brought in, I would like to raise a matter. The Chamber is seized by the Prosecution's supplemental motion for leave to amend its 65 ter exhibit list with two additional exhibits, filed on the 27th of May. I would first like to clarify something. Perhaps there is a mistake or an error in the numbering of the intercept transcripts. If I understood you correctly, Mr. Vanderpuye, you were asking for admission of intercept number 524, but the Appendix A, there is only the English translation of number 523. In B/C/S there is the original with number 523 and 524. I would like to clarify with you, 523 is already an exhibit on the 65 ter list but not 524. Is that a mistake, or is there a translation? Perhaps you can try to figure that out. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, and good morning to Your Honours, everyone. If you can just bear with me one second. I'd to just look at the appendix and I can give you a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And in the meantime, Mr. Tolimir, I will then ask you if you have a comment to this Prosecution's motion for adding these two documents to the 65 ter exhibit list. First we ask the Prosecution for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I've looked at the appendix. It appears to be an error, but I'd like to confirm that with my colleague, because it relates to, I believe, his witness, and I think he will know more certainly whether it is, in fact, an error than I would. So if you could give us till the break, I can come back to you with a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No problem with that. I wanted to raise this problem as early as possible so that you have the time to clarify the situation. And I will then at a later stage ask you, Mr. Tolimir, for your comments to this motion of the Prosecution. Could the witness be brought in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please sit down. Please sit down. Again, good morning. Now we can start. I would like to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies, and I would like to remind all speakers to switch off the microphone while the witness is answering. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Yesterday when we left off I had asked you some questions about the possibility of intercepting VRS communications in light of the attitude towards security of those communications by speakers and VRS officers that are the subject of those intercepts, but I'd like to focus you, if I could, on more technical aspects of that security. What I'd like to know is, in your experience, did the VRS use the means at their disposal in order to secure the communications from a technical point of view, such as engaging in masking techniques or reducing the power of communications, the use of cryptographic devices and that sort of thing. If you could just tell us a little bit about that.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say from my experience is that in the former JNA there existed standard procedures about camouflage, anti-electronic protection, and they were used to the extent of our ability in view of the fact that we had a larger state in the past with a certain depth and a certain width -- width so that interception and listening of this kind was rather difficult. Let me stress --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should pause a moment because there seems to be a technical problem with the screen. Is that correct? Mr. Gajic, what is the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the problem is we can't hear the witness. We can't hear the witness on the B/C/S channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That problem should be solved by a technician very soon. You have to wait for that. The normal channel is not working. Could you please say something so that we can find out if the translation is to be heard by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three. One, two. Testing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you -- perhaps, Mr. Vanderpuye, you could ask the next question and we will hear the witness answering, and then we can figure out if it is working.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. He hadn't finished his answer, actually, to the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll do my best. It was very poorly phrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I had asked you about whether or not the VRS had taken advantage of the technical means at their disposal in order to -- in order to secure radio relay communications, and you were answering about that. If you could expand on your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you answer, was the translation to be heard on the B/C/S channel? Mr. Gajic, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can hear the interpretation. We could hear the interpretation before. We just couldn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Please answer the question of the Prosecutor, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I had begun to say, the Army of Republika Srpska had a set of protective measures it was using. I believe I spoke about that yesterday. There were protected channels, secure channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, but we have to stop at the moment because there is no technical connection to -- in the B/C/S channel to the Defence. We need a technician, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask the witness to say something so we can check if it's working now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat and count until -- up until --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Testing, testing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it now working? Okay. Let us continue. I had to stop you in the middle of your answer. I'm very sorry. I apologise, but please continue if you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've been saying, the Army of Republika Srpska had a set of protective measures. The first one was working on ranges that we were not able to follow, primarily the SMC range from 4.4 to 4.8 and 4.8 to 5 gigahertz. The next thing, they also had supporting equipment and secure channels. According to our knowledge, those channels went from the General Staff of the VRS to Belgrade and the subordinated corps. We were not able to monitor these channels. And third, there were analogue channels that most of them used that we were able to monitor and we did monitor. Also it happened that through the fault of operators or other personnel, we were sometimes able to monitor even encrypted channels because they released telegrams that had been encrypted in open communication, and then we would capture it. There were also measures that were standard in telecommunications, using code-names, using tables for identification, using identification numbers, et cetera. All these are very well-known techniques, and everyone was familiar with them. However, they didn't always comply. They didn't always apply them. There were also communications they tried to mask by television channels. For instance, you would make contact near a television broadcasting station and try to establish communication. Also, throughout this period personnel rotated. You could see from yesterday's report that people were warned repeatedly. What does that tell us? If operators were warning officers and other personnel, that means that mistakes happened. There were many other things that I could say, but I don't want to burden the Court because it's very technical. In any case, the conclusion is very simple: It's very clear that there were things we were able to listen to and other things we were not able to listen to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned before we had the technical difficulty something about camouflaging, and I don't know if that is the same as what you've just discussed concerning television channels, but if you could explain that to Court -- to the Court that would be helpful. And also I'd like you to explain to the Court what the impact is on the strength of broadcasting in terms of your unit's ability to intercept.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the devices that the VRS had were 40 to 50 years old. I went to school 30 years ago, and I trained on these old RRU-800 devices. That means that they were practically obsolete. They could work with full strength or diminished strength like 50 per cent, but it's my opinion that they never used diminished capacity because that would have been one-third of their ability. So they always operated with 70 to 80 per cent strength, which at that time was their full strength. As for masking or camouflage, it was mostly used not to interfere with secure channels. For instance, you would establish a link near a television station, and we had no equipment for jamming.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is there any tactical military advantage to be gained from transmitting a radio signal at full strength as opposed to transmitting a radio strength at somewhat of a lesser strength?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my point of view, from what I know, in order to have a secure communication without any breakdowns, you always use full strength. If you are talking about important things, about important operations and you want to transmit the information properly, you would normally use full strength so that your subordinate would understand you correctly and comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is the danger of that the possibility that that communication may exceed the distance that it's intended to reach and actually be intercepted by someone else?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained. Every manufacturer provides supporting documentation indicating the technical specifications of devices. We learnt that at school. There are advantages and disadvantages of every device. We went to the same schools. Mathematically, you can dispute certain things, but in practice it's not so. The manufacturer provides certain specifications and says he guarantees communication. For instance, in the case of RRU-800, the guarantee is for an 80 kilometre distance with one antenna and up to 50 kilometres with another type of antenna. That means that the manufacturer guarantees that at the distance of 80 kilometres communication will be possible. That doesn't mean that communication will necessarily reach 130 kilometres. Electromagnetic waves are not a live creature. They spread in space. They have a certain degree of beaming. They have a vertical and horizontal strength. It has direct and lateral range, and the range in practice was greater, but it also depended on the hour of the day, on the weather conditions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that, Witness. I'd like to take you to a completely different area for just a moment, and then I want to show you a map, and I'd like to have you explain that to the Trial Chamber. But before we do that, I want to ask you, after your testimony in the Popovic case, were you retained by the Office of the Prosecutor as a consultant in -- in the practice of interception?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean when I was there at that time or subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: After you testified in the Popovic case, were you retained by the Office of the Prosecutor as a consultant?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was -- what was the purpose of that? If you could just briefly explain.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They needed some kind of estimate and analysis of the possibility of intercepting VRS communications. That analysis had been done by a Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to review that analysis?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was three years ago, I believe. I think I still remember parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you assist the Prosecution in understanding that analysis, that expert analysis?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can very briefly say a few words about that analysis, although I am not an official forensic expert. That report had been done by an expert, who was very good in his field, but his analysis was directed at one objective only, to prove that it was absolutely impossible to intercept communications. First of all, the man put in completely different -- wrong data. He shortened the distance between different hubs of communications by 10 to 20 kilometres. He put in the strength of usage of 50 per cent, and if we know that their full strength was 70 per cent, then it was considerably diminished compared to reality. He ignored the fact that we used makeshift antennas, which after 1996, after the war, were directed towards the west, and based on these measurements he used his own mathematical calculations and tried to prove that we were wrong. When that failed, he presented completely different documents indicating completely different frequencies. He presented a whole table of code-names from 1994 and locations of different hubs of communications. I'm not going to go into detail but he used completely inaccurate information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has an objection. The Prosecutor did not include onto the 65 ter list the documentation that both he and the witness have been referring to, and he did not put us on notice that this would be discussed. Based on what he just said, it is clear that the witness cannot be objective since he appears also as a Prosecution advisor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. I think that the Chamber will consider this clearly, and I think it is interesting information we just received about the role of this witness for the Prosecution. Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And just so the record is clear, the Defence was provided with a very detailed explanation of this witness's involvement with the Prosecution as a consultant in May of 1997, sent to them on the 21st of May, and it details specifically the kinds of information that the witness assisted the Prosecution analysing in this very complex interception report. In terms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of your objectivity, Witness, has your engagement as a consultant with the Prosecution in May of 2007 and your review of the report of the Defence expert in the Popovic case in any way affected your testimony here today or shaded the way you've presented matters of fact?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't understand the question correctly. I don't remember this as clearly, and I'm testifying on the basis of my memory back from those days. I worked in the company of officers who had graduated from the military academy in Belgrade and specialised in PEB, that's to say counter-electronic warfare, and they were the ones working with me on this analysis. We did not discover anything new. I only examined the data and matched it, the data in the Defence report, that is, and concluded that it was inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. And for your consultancy with the Office of the Prosecutor, can you tell us how long that engagement lasted?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, five to six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you receive any remuneration for that period of time?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that. What I received was to cover for my stay here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Do you know approximately how much that was?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you precisely. Perhaps a thousand or a thousand five hundred convertible marks or $1.000. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Are you testifying here today with the expectation that you may be retained in the future as a consultant again with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you have an expectation that you'll be retained as a Prosecutor [sic] if you testify here today?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to take you to a different area, and that concerns the map that I promised to show you. It's 65 ter 911.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm told that the technic is very slow today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, I can go to another -- well, I can't, actually. I'm afraid I have to wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm optimistic it is coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we could zoom in a little bit at the title of it just so that the witness can see it and identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to see the title of this map? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a map that I believe was made back in 1998 or 1999 at the request of the ICTY Prosecution. It was done by the 2nd Corps command. In fact, this is a copy of the situation as it existed based on the intercepts of communications of the Army of Republika Srpska from the period between January and September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd just like to go over with you some of the symbols in this -- in this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just zoom in on the triangle in the middle of the screen right now and blow that up a little bit. A bit more. Right there. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have a number of symbols in this triangle, and if you need me to make it bigger just let me know so that we can -- so that you can explain this clearly as possible, but we have a number of symbols on this diagram. The first I'd like to -- the first thing I'd like to address, though, is some writing under the line. It's in the middle of the screen. And can you tell us what that says? And if you need it to be bigger, just let us know.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Below the longest line, you mean, in the middle of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that the path was established after the NATO strike, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And is that what the situation was in 1995, that this map -- that you've indicated this map is intended to represent?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that in 1995, for every particular month, the PEB department produced analyses of the communication links used by the VRS. The analyses examined each and every path, what sort of devices it used, across which channels, and it was constantly updated. This specific path is one that I cannot recall at this time. It is an alternative to the path which ran across Ozren. I may be mistaken, but after the NATO strikes, when they destroyed Kraljica, "the Queen," soon thereafter this path was established. Other than that, it had not been active during the war through to the end of 1995. It was active across Ozren and established from an SMC, so we weren't able to follow, to monitor that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When was the NATO strike that's referred to in this diagram? When did it occur?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier that there were strikes in Bosnia toward the end of the war, and then there were strikes in Serbia in 1999, and they targeted hubs of communication in Serbia. I can't be more specific than that. It's been 15 years, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And if you could just take us through -- if we could zoom out just a little bit, and if you could just take us through ... all right, what these lines are that run all the way across the map. What do they represent first?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lines marked on this map are the radio relay links along which the waves propagated, and as such they are imagined to exist like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do they show the manner of communication that occurred among links that pre-existed the war, or do they show communications, radio communication -- a radio communication network that existed only after the war?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These lines indicate the links as they existed in the summer of 1995, except for the path that I've referred to a moment ago. Most of the radio relay links existed before the war. I've already said that these were, for the most part, stationary facilities, communications facilities which belonged to the former JNA and subsequently to the VRS, and if one of these hubs goes out of work, another one pops up and is switched on in its stead. So that's the sort of a network that existed in Bosnia and Serbia. This particular map indicates the situation in 1995 and demonstrates the links that we monitored. Not all of them, however, because there were platoons at the level of the division which intercepted communications, and there were also departments dealing with the same matter in all the brigades, which covered specific paths within their own areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me focus you in, if I can, on the bottom right-hand corner of this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we could zoom more tightly, yes, on the cluster of lines that are centred. If you could just blow that up a little bit, please. All right. Just a bit more, please. Okay. That's very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like for you to mark this map, so I'll ask for a pen to be given to you, but while that's happening could you just describe what's on here. If we start with the triangle in the middle, you can see the words "Panorama 99" there, near the triangle. Could you tell us what the triangle itself represents?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The triangle in the middle is a symbol used by the former Yugoslav People's Army standing for the radio relay hub or node at Veliki Zep. In Yugoslavia it was planned to be a communications centre in the event of a war. These symbols were something that was taken over from the documentation of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Inside the triangle that you've just circled, you can see the number 800 and then the number 1. I don't know if you -- maybe you can't see it that well. Maybe we can blow it up a little. But can you tell us what number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you blow it up you will lose the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I thought that might be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just tell us what the number indicates.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. The number -- or, rather, let me first say that the radio relay hub is a stationary facility which radiates a number of links. So it is not just an intermediate station, meaning that there would be one link coming into it and one out of it. Now, 1 means that they were -- the paths were established with RRU-1, and the other number means that they were established by RRU-800. 800, that is, means that they were established by RRU-800. You will see that were also SMC 130S which were used to establish the path to Cer, and then you will also see that we have SMC 130 as the path leading to Strazbenica and onwards. Strazbenica was another radio relay hub covering the Hercegovina Corps. So it went from Strazbenica to Jahorina and to Pale. The final lines leading in various directions stand for the connecting paths between radio relay hubs and brigade commands for the most part. The curving line, the winding line, to the left stands for the wire link. The VRS Main Staff had, in addition to the RRU-1 path, also a wire path connecting it directly to the Veliki Zep radio relay hub.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If you could, I'd like to have you mark a few things on this map. First with respect to the last thing you spoke of, which is the wire line, can you just draw an arrow along that line indicating what it is? So you draw a wire line from Veliki Zep to the Main Staff showing where the wire communication is. You can put the letter W next to it so that we know what it is.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the wire link, the connection between Veliki Zep and Han Pijesak, then this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you could indicate which the SMC lines were on this -- on this diagram. If you can't, I can -- we can do it on another one. And if you could write SMC next to that.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The one that you've written SMC on that goes in a northerly direction, where does it go to? Is that the one that goes to Strazbenica or is that one that goes to another location?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska could hardly be able to establish radio relay links without relying on the hubs in Serbia. So it definitely used those. The top line indicates the SMC path between Veliki Zep and Mount Cer where another radio relay hub was located which redirected signals onto the main hub at Avala, near Belgrade, which also had a wire connection with the VJ Main Staff. And other path was the alternative leading to east across Svinjari, Trebava, Kozara, on to Banja Luka, but this isn't something that we can see on the map. This other SMC path is the so-called southern path leading to Strazbenica and on to Jahorina. It also led from Strazbenica to Veliki Tmur. I think that there was another path leading to Serbia which I believe is called Cigota. The documents we used to have indicate that there was another section leading to Vlasic, where the TV Sarajevo journalist was killed, and on to Klekovo and Pljesevica. In other words, there had to exist alternative routes for all these. I said there was another location in addition to Cer which was near Cacak or Uzice, and I think this was established with the SMC set which means that we weren't able to monitor it. In other words, this -- this was the skeleton of the lines which kept the whole system working. Now, how were we aware of these facilities? Well, we had a number of officers who had worked in these facilities before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's just focus in on the map for the moment. Let's just focus in on what's in the screen on front of us for a moment, just for this -- for this part. You can see here a triangle on the left of the screen that says the word "Zlatar." Do you know what that means? It's on the top left corner of the map in front of you. What does that stand for and what does it mean, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to see, the symbol stands for the terminal radio relay system in the area of Vlasenica. This is a code-name for the Drina Corps, as, in fact, it says here. It had eight channels with the radio relay hub at Zep, that's to say, with the superior command and subordinate brigades. And I'm referring to the path running between Zlatar and Veliki Zep. This path was established from the device RRU-800.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear for the purposes of this map, could you put a VZ next to Veliki Zep so that we can see where it is.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Below where you've written that, you can see a triangle to the right that has the word "Uran" on it. Do you know what that is and what it means?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can see here is the terminal radio relay station, which was a provisional one set up for a certain period. It says: "During the operations at Zep in the range of RRU-1." I think I remember it was our estimate that it was the same device that had operated in the area of Pribicevac, and after the operation in Srebrenica, the command moved the device into the Zepa area. But I'm not saying this for a fact because we didn't have a station for technical analysis of signals, but it's typical that as soon as it stopped working in Pribicevac, the very next day the same frequency occurred in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think we can go to another part of this map. Can you just indicate for the record where the Main Staff of the VRS is located, and just put an MS next to it.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff, according to our information, was in Han Pijesak. This is based purely on the intelligence gathered by interception.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the radio relay nodes that you've circled on this map, were those areas that your units were able to intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see the frequencies indicated here. They were written down and recorded. That means that we were able to monitor them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear, one other thing for this map. If you could put a circle around Uran, the triangle that we were just talking about, and if you could write next to that it "Zepa" so it's clear for the record what you have associated with it.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this marked exhibit at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This marked map will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P279.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks. If we could start again with -- with the full map, and I'd like to go to a different section of it, because it's rather large.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which part of the map do you want to have on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. I'd like to have the right-hand corner again, but a little bit more to the right this time. That's right, embracing the entire corner. If we could blow that up just a little bit to the -- if you could start just a little bit left of where the lines converge. Not all the way in the corner but just a little bit to the left and all the way to the right so we can blow that up. Perfect. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to see the markings on this side of the map? You can see on the right-hand side "Badem," and over there you see a triangle with 1 and 800 in it. Then you can see beneath that "Bratunacka Brigada." Then you can see "IKM DK." Are you able to see it, or should we blow that up so that you can see it better?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And let's start with Badem. Over there see 1 and 800. Does that apply in the same way as you've indicated for the triangle at Veliki Zep, that is, it uses RRU-1 and RRU-800 communications?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can see here, and that's contemporaneous, that was the terminal radio relay station in the area of Bratunac. There's the code-name of the Bratunac Brigade, Badem, and it had a direct connection with the radio relay node Veliki Zep and further on towards the Drina Corps command. Also, there was an alternative one-channel back-up device, RRU-1, which communicated with Veliki Zep from this communication hub.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You made a reference to Pribicevac a little earlier in one of your answers. Are you able to indicate where that is on this map?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So you've drawn a circle around it now, and it embraces the triangle number 1. Could you put a letter P in there.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in order to have communication between the Drina Corps command at Zlatar, which is all the way on the left side of this screen, and the communication with the Drina Corps IKM at Pribicevac, was that communication able to occur directly or did it have to pass through Veliki Zep?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, knowing the topography of the area around Srebrenica, to put it quite simply, it's a complete wilderness. Only animals live there. It's hunting grounds. Our men, soldiers, discovered that radio relay route using RRU-1, which is easily mobile, and it used the frequencies 259 to 275 megahertz. It says that on the 22nd January 1995, the forward command post was set up for the Skelani brigade, and an extension, 311, was installed, and by dialling three digits, could you connect directly to the command of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica. We monitored this connection constantly after we discovered it, because it was somehow illogical to set up a forward command post in such a wilderness knowing that Srebrenica was a protected area, and that that type of communication should be set up there was not really obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'm a little unclear about your answer, though. Is it that -- well, let me ask maybe if you can clarify it. When you dial the extension from the command to get the forward command post, does that telephone or that radio connection go directly to the forward command post or does it pass through Veliki Zep or some other location, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there was no optic visibility between Pribicevac and Vlasenica, that connection had a linkage path through Veliki Zep and on to Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think we can go to another -- if I could tender this, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P280.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should be aware of the time. You've now used, including our technical problems, one hour and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go to the map. That's fine. And if we could just blow-up the right-hand side a little bit larger, though, this time. A little bit more northerly as well. We have to make a selection, I think, larger than this. A bit larger than that, just to catch the angle on the right-hand side of the screen. In the middle, you'll see -- on the right-hand side you'll see an angle. If you can catch that in the square then we'll be fine. Okay. And if we could -- if we could make it a little bit less to the left because that's not so important for this. A little bit more north and a little bit more to the right. You see the angle on the top? That's what I want to catch in this frame. Okay. Almost. That's it. Right there. Just that right half of the screen up until the corner on the right-hand side. If we capture that, that will be perfect. All right. We can work with this. Just go down a little bit. Down more. Keep going. Keep going. Keep going. Stop. Stop, stop, stop. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I know it's a bit small, but if you look where the letter SMC is -- where the letters SMC are, can you tell us -- yes. Is that the -- interesting. The SMC line that you've indicated before, that goes to a place called Ka Avali. Can you tell us where that is?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't understood -- understand your question. What place did you mean, in the north? This line, at least that's our assumption, is a relay connecting Veliki Zep in Bosna and Herzegovina with the radio relay node Cer, in Serbia, using an SMC 130. From that radio relay node one connection went to Avala, Mount Avala, and it was also used to achieve a radio relay connection through Gucevo with the Zvornik Brigade. That's the south-west line, the thicker one, and the finer one leading to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks. For the Mount Avala node, could you just indicate that with a circle, and S for Serbia. And then I'd ask you to do the same for Gucevo and then for Zvornik. Are you able to see that on the map or ...

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see everything except Mount Avala.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, we can't see Gucevo on the map. So if you could circle it and write Gucevo or G next to it that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you show us where the Zvornik Brigade is, if you can see it? And put a Z next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And right below the word -- the letter Z that you've written is the word "Palma." Can you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the code-name of the Zvornik Brigade in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the circle that you put G around says "Brana 1999." Can you tell us about that? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information and intelligence, although there must be more precise information, it a radio relay station that the Zvornik Brigade manned in order to connect with the Drina Corps. Since there was no optic visibility from Zvornik, they couldn't connect with Serbia directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And between Mount Avala and Gucevo you can see a line which is -- where the numbers 200 and 800 are written. Can you tell us what that is? I think 800 we have pretty clear, but what does 200 mean?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the communication systems of the VRS and the Army of Yugoslavia, there was another device, FM-200, that worked in the range of 400 to 500 megahertz. That's our estimate, because we could catch the signal but we couldn't monitor it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Then could you just write the name of the device next to the number 200, please, on this map.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then to the left there's a line that extends downward where 24/800 is written. Could you explain what that is -- or what that means. I'm sorry. It's towards the middle of the image, at the top of your screen.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a radio relay communication set up for the requirements of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. From what we know, it went from Bijeljina to the Banj [phoen] hill, right here at Mount Majevica, and on towards Majevica Brigades. Number 24 means they worked with 24 channels using the RRU-800 device.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Were any of your interception units or facilities able to intercept the Zvornik Brigade or the node in Zvornik or the node in Gucevo or the node at Mount Avala?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were able to listen to them from both installations, the route Vlasenica-Veliki Zep, or Cer-Gucevo. We were able to listen. This route from Mount Cer towards Crni Vrh, that is Gucevo, if you extend the line it will land precisely within the range of the Konjuh installation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I would like to tender this marked map, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This map will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P281.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can go to the larger map again. I just want to focus in on the route if we can catch it. We'll have to go to the right-hand corner again, starting up a little bit. Up. Stop. From there all the way down to bottom on the right-hand -- that's fine, I think. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to see and can you draw for us the route from the Drina Corps command to the Zvornik Brigade as you were able to capture it in 1995? If you can trace that out for us.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, that connection was made from the Vlasenica area towards Veliki Zep, then Cer, Gucevo, and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was it possible, as far as you're aware, in 1995, to have a direct communication between Zvornik and the Drina Corps command without going through this route?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say it for a fact, but a direct connection between Vlasenica and Zvornik was not possible with a radio relay connection without relying on a -- on a node.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were your interception units able to intercept communications going towards Pale or going towards Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, we had frequencies that came from the south. On a larger map you could probably see it, that a wave beamed from Mount Jahorina could very easily be received at the Konjuh installation. I cannot see anything here, it's a different kind of map, but we have reports of such intercepts, and we have also indicated frequencies that went to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you're able to, can you approximate where -- actually, we'll leave it like this. I would like to tender this and I'll go to a different area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P282.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President. I'd also like to tender the large map itself. It's 65 ter 911, I believe. Yes, 911.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P283.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to draw your attention to a different area, if I could, at this point, and that relates to the notebooks that were received by the -- by the Office of the Prosecutor. Now, do you know -- were you involved in the transfer of those notebooks to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved with the section for gathering information on the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us where the notebooks were before they were transferred to the Office of the Prosecutor, if you could in brief terms.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other notebooks remained, as far as I remember, in the depot at the northern site, because in end 1997, I came again to the PED section of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were they kept there throughout the period of time once they had been filled out and collected, were they continually kept in one place?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The notebooks were first on the sites, the northern site and the southern site. When they were filled, they were returned to the installation at Tuzla, where the command of the unit was based, and then sometime in 1996 or 1997 the installation at Tuzla was closed down and the whole unit was transferred to the northern site. And the notebooks were transferred as well. And from there, when the investigators arrived, they were brought to the command of the 2nd Corps and they were handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 65 ter 855.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We shouldn't broadcast this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, this is a document that's dated 24th April 1998. It purports a transfer of 135 documents, and I'll refer you to paragraph 2 of the document. Were you involved in that transfer? It was to a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see I was involved, but I was not alone. There was a whole group. I just represented that group on behalf of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were those documents actually transferred to the Office of the Prosecutor, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just a cover letter for a set of documents, and the cover letter indicates the total number of documents handed over. There is a signature here, but I believe there's another supporting document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Under seal, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 855 will be Exhibit P284, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness -- I'd like to show the witness 65 ter 862.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it's a cover -- or, rather, it's a letter accompanying the earlier record, and it contains a list of every document handed over to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we should go to the last page of this document. It should be page -- I think it's page 5 in e-court. We're not broadcasting it are we? Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Do you recognise -- do you recognise your signature at the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the last number of the documents handed over here is 135, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The numbers that are written just after the enumeration, for example, 134, 135, the numbers that are written to right of that, strictly confidential numbers, do those correspond to entries in the notebooks that you've spoken about before?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a number of different pieces of information contained here which indicate the entries in the notebooks save for 133 and 135, which relate to individual sheets of paper that we bound together and indicated that they totaled 68 [as interpreted] sheets.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And these strictly confidential numbers that are written down here, do they correspond what is written inside the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Only the notebooks had such numbers written in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document as well. I think it should also be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P285, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it is time for the break. Mr. President, I just want to inform the Court that I have about five more documents to go through for the purposes of chain of custody and then I'll be finished with my direct examination with the leave of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have the first break now and we will resume at 11.00. The Court Officer will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The first thing I wanted to mention to you is in relation to the question you'd asked about the error concerning our filing. In fact, it is an error, and we will be filing a corrigendum shortly. As I understand it, also we have a hard copy of the correct translation available for the Trial Chamber should it wish to examine it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have received it in the meantime. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. The second thing is that there is a correction, I believe, that has been made in the transcript. It looks like page 29, line 17. Page 29, line 17, which indicates the witness's answer concerned a document which contains 68 sheets and that should be 80 -- actually, the typewritten version of it says 83 sheets. I believe the witness said 86. So that should be corrected. At least the transcript should be corrected to reflect what he said. The document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you clarify that with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I think I can. Just a moment. Let me get the P number for that one. I think it was -- it was 65 ter 862, so it's P285. And if we could have that in e-court, just so I can show it to the witness. He could take a look at the document. And if we could go to the last page, I think it was page 5 of this document, and blow-up the very bottom of it where you can see the number 135.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The B/C/S version disappeared again. We had it on the screen already.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't know if we're able to blow it up. If we can't, that's okay. We have the English translation anyway. And I think under -- in row 135, we can see it refers to radio interceptor daily report, and next to that immediately you can see it says 83 sheets and then 83 documents. So I just want to clarify with the witness what he said in reference to row 135. So if he can see that, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. I can see now that it's 83. At first glance I thought it was 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that, Witness. I'd like to show you 65 ter 858.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This also shouldn't be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a document that's dated 10th May 1999, and it shows that material was handed over to an investigating team at The Hague consisting of A5 format notebooks, 55, and then it says original transcripts of conversation A4 format notebooks, 1 piece, as well as 1.4 megabyte diskettes and a shift diary kept by an individual. Witness, do you recall being involved in the transfer of these materials?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the orders of my superior, I handed the material over. He authorised me to sign the document and give it to the person named herein.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, with respect to the -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P286, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, with respect to the 1.4 megabyte diskettes, are those consistent with the types of diskettes that were used in respect of the interception operation of your units?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were 1.4 megabyte diskettes that were mostly used at cryptographic stations and probably contained typed reports. I can't recall exactly what they contain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If could I have the witness shown, please, 65 ter 1644.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a document that's also from the 2nd Corps command, and it relates to the hand-over of certain material on 14th May 1999. Now, if we go to the second page of this document, we can see the individuals that were involved in this transfer. Do you have any recollection of this transfer or were you involved in the transfer in any way?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I know approximately when this was handed over, but I myself did not take part in it. It was a different department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document not be admitted through this witness if the -- if the document was not authored by or handed over by the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I believe that that's -- that's a fair question to put once I've finished using the document if I intend to tender it, but I do intend to establish a sufficient foundation for its admission. So I would submit that the question is premature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At the very -- if we could go to the next page in the English translation. We'll stay on the B/C/S page. You can see that items 46, 47, and 48 refer to the transfer of transcripts of conversations in A5-size notebooks, 55 pieces; transcripts of conversations in A4-size notebooks, 1 piece; and taped conversations on 1.4 megabyte diskettes, 2 pieces. Do you have any knowledge of those documents being transferred in relation to your intercept operation?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I did not take part in the drafting of this record. My department was charged only with handing over documents that were the result of intercepting. This is a collated record made by the then superior officer. These were documents originating from other departments, including the items listed here under 46, 47, 48, which -- and 49, which came from my department and which were the subject of the earlier document we looked at. Now, the material listed under 50 did not come from my department.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On that basis, Mr. President, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The decision lies in your hands. I understand the witness said that he did not produce the document. Was it someone else? Well, I don't know. The witness stated that he did not take part in the hand-over, and that's the extent of my submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that this witness was not involved in the handing over of the documents and was not in a position to identify parts of this document, so that the Prosecution should consider another way to tender this document if it seems to be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you can see the date of this document was 14 May 1999, which is four days after the transfer that you testified that you participated in. To your knowledge, does the 50 -- do the 55 A5 notebooks and one A4-size notebook and two diskettes reflect the material that you were involved in transferring to the representatives from the Hague?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I most definitely handed over the 55 A5-size notebook, one A4-size notebook to Ms. Stefanie Frease. What happened most probably was that she took that record and combined it with the records of other documents handed over from other departments and that's how this record came about. But I can also state that I did not take part in the process leading up to this particular record.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. President, I would note that -- I'm just going to find the exhibit number. The entries that are in 46, 47, and 48 of this document, and 49, correspond almost verbatim to P286, which was the document I qualified prior to presenting the witness with this one. Just so the record is clear as to that, and I can show it to the Trial Chamber if you'd like to see it again, but if you look at entries on this document, 46 - the 55 pieces, A5 size; A4 size, one piece; two pieces concerning the disks or the agenda or shift diary of that individual - you'll see that reflected verbatim in the exhibit that I've just -- that is, P286 that I've just tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful if we can see that on the screen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't know if it's possible, but it would be great if we put this translation up on the left side and put in P286 just in English so the Trial Chamber can see exactly that and can juxtapose one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have only the two translations on the screen. We wanted to have the first one. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And I think if you can compare items 1, 2, 3 and 4 on the right with items 46, 47, 48, and 49 on the left you'll see that -- well, they're identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could just go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes. As I understand you, you are trying to introduce the document on the left as part of your evidence through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: But this witness has said he did not author it and he was not involved in the transfer of this particular bundle of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's -- that's right too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think I can see your difficulty, but I'm wondering whether you needed to be belabour the point to introduce this document through this witness. Why not through the person who has signed there?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it can be done both ways, to be -- to be honest. I think it can be introduced through this witness, because the document itself encompasses the materials with -- which the witness has said he handed over to a representative of the -- of The Hague Tribunal, and that is a document that is already in evidence. It's P286. So even though this witness didn't author the document, he has testified that the document, in fact, reflects the materials that he handed over that is shown in P286. That's the reason why it's relevant to introduce it through him. Not because he authored it and not because he didn't author it or he didn't sign it, but the document itself reflects the physical materials that he was involved in handing over. That's the reason why I've had them put on the -- in e-court at the same time so we can see that they are the same documents, and it's part of the chain of the transfer of that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do not intend to challenge anything or create complications for Mr. Vanderpuye. I wish to draw your attention to one logical matter. If this witness handed over only four documents listed here under 46 through to 49, it is illogical for him to be used for the admission of the remaining 45 documents he knows nothing of. I do not dispute that the documents containing these particular contents listed here under 46 to 49 should be admitted through him, but I don't think he should be used for the rest. I think the witness said clearly two times that he was not involved in their hand-over. Of course, it will be up to the Trial Chamber to make a decision on the Prosecution's motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I respond for a moment. I think Mr. Tolimir's conflated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think Mr. Tolimir's conflated two issues. I'm not seeking to introduce the notebooks through this document; I'm seeking to introduce the document itself because the document is a record of custody of the materials, of the notebooks. So if the notebooks went to one person and then to another person and then to another person and then wound up at the Tribunal, all of those records are essential and relevant to the chain of custody, and that's what this document shows. It shows that the 55 notebooks went from one person to another person and then to the person at the Tribunal, and that's the reason for its relevance. Even if the witness didn't write the document, didn't author the document, or even didn't see the document, as long as he can say that those notebooks are the notebooks that he handled in the chain of custody, then it is appropriate and relevant -- it is appropriate and relevant evidence of that fact, of the record of transfer, not the documents -- I'm not seeking to tender the documents through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Nothing in my objection had to do with notebooks. I only referred to the four documents listed on the right-hand side which, as can be seen clearly, the witness himself handed over to the representative of the Tribunal and not a representative of his army, but it is illogical for him to be used for the admission of a document listing a number of other sets of material that he was not involved with. I did not mention notebooks at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: After having considered the situation, the Chamber is of the view that the statement of the witness on page 35, line 3 through 8, is essential and he stated that he personally handed over, as he is recollecting that, four items of this long list of documents to Ms. Stefanie Frease, a representative of the OTP. Taking into account this statement of the witness, we will receive this document to have a full picture of the chain of custody of the -- especially these four parts of the documents, so that at the end of the day we can give weight to that, how these documents, the notebooks, came from the custody of his unit to the OTP of this Tribunal. It will be received. If I remember correctly, it was tendered under seal. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: P286 should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is under seal, but the new document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The new document doesn't need to be. I don't think there's any specific reference to the witness in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1644 is now Exhibit P287.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show the witness, if I may, 65 ter 859.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to have the witness shown 65 ter 859, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is this the document on the screen you were asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, we have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, this is a document that is from the 2nd Corps. It indicates from the G-2 department. It's dated 13 December 2000, and it purports that there was a transfer of additional materials here consisting of, among other things, 42 pieces, it says "station diaries with data collected by EIV," electronic reconnaissance, and also 7 pieces 1.44 megabyte disks with data collected by electronic reconnaissance. And then there are some other documents. It says review of radio surveillance reports, dated 1 August to 30 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go to the next -- to Annex -- Annex 2. That's two pages up in the English. And I think it's also two pages up in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First of all, are you aware of a transfer of the station diaries, 42 pieces of these, in -- in 2000 from the G-2 unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say I'm familiar with these documents. It's highly probable - in fact, there was no one else - that we handed the technical operation and the superior commander authorised this with his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the strictly confidential numbers, dates that are indicated in this Annex 2, do those correspond to the methodology or the manner in which the intercept notebooks that were generated by your department were documented?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that fits. It corresponds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And let me show you Annex 3 of this document. That's on the next page, I think both in the B/C/S and in -- and in the English. Can you tell us what this EIV abbreviation means?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Electronic reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was your unit engaged in that activity?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you can see here that these are for January through -- it looks like November of 1995 -- December of 1995, I should say, in various -- various parts among the seven disks. Would that correspond to the types of disks that were used by your unit in -- in doing the intercept -- intercepting -- in intercepting communications?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you say whether or not these materials as reflected in this document came from your unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On that basis, Mr. President, I would like to tender this document as well into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P288.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness 65 ter 0 -- I'm sorry, 856, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you have on the screen in front of you now is a record of transfer of archival material gathered through ER regarding events in Srebrenica 1995, and it indicates that a representative of the Tribunal, Jack Hunter, and representatives of the G-2 and 2nd Corps command selected and made a list of tapes from 1995. Let me ask you, Mr. Witness, were you involved in the transfer of these tapes?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the preparation of these recordings I was involved, and I was partially involved in the hand-over. However, I was not a signatory. But I did accompany this gentleman who visited the northern location. He inspected the equipment. He listened to some intercepts from that period. And there was a whole team working down there in the hall of veterans, and we selected some magnetic tapes that they reviewed, and I believe they were supposed to go somewhere else and continue their job. So we packed these tapes into a cardboard case, taped it and signed, both of us, so that he could inspect it a few days later, see that it hasn't been tampered with, and he carried it further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Of the tapes that you packed, were these a total of 19 tapes as is indicated in this document, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it says 19, that means there were 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, on that basis I would tender this document also into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P289.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness 65 ter 863, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, what you have in front of you is a tape -- a photograph of a tape, or a photocopy of a photograph of a tape, indicating number 48/Q2, and then it has an ERN number, T000-0471. First of all, do you recognise the label that is on the tape at the bottom in the photograph, where it says 48 -- 08/2-01 and it looks like 4 -- 144.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is our marking, but the handwritten note at the top, that's not something we wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. I'd just like to -- I think we can go through just a couple of pages of this before I move to tender it. If we could go to page 2. I just want to show you the back side of this tape. Is that your marking, by the way, the label that's on it?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And if I can show you page 3. Do you recognise what this shows?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is a cardboard box where these tapes were placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to page 4. I want to show you the other side of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we could rotate it that would be helpful. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's on this?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before, in the old Yugoslavia, in every municipality, on the occasion of Tito's birthday, there was a big festivity involving athletics and other performances by pupils and teenagers. There were a number of exercises, always accompanied by music, and I even recognise some people here. Professor Mikic, who worked at the faculty of sports. Then Professor Meho Alic-Partic. And this is a floppy disk [as interpreted] that we received. I remember this technician, Suljo, who still works there. This was taken from Radio Tuzla. Of course, the contents was immediately erased so we can use it for recording intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. In the transcript there's -- it records that you said the word "floppy disk." I just want to confirm what you were referring to. It's page 44, line 25. Did you refer to floppy disk, or did you refer to tape?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a magnetic tape or a diskette tape. We can call it whatever we like.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Can you confirm that the box and the tape, in fact, are the product of your unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this as well into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, that will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P290.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness 65 ter 863. Oh, sorry, 864. This shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, what I'm showing you now is a note that was found inside the box 48 that we've just seen. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, before the hand-over we received an order from the superior commander to re-listen to these magnetic tapes and to record some typical signs, indications, locations, participants, place names, as we can see here. This is a description of the contents of each magnetic tape and the signature of the person who did the listening. And this description is also placed in the box, together with the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, with respect to the tapes and the notebooks, were they ever transferred from the place where they were held to any other location before they were turned over to the -- to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that notebooks were taken from the sites to a place near Tuzla, and when the unit was transferred they were taken to the northern location. Also, the tapes were taken from the southern location, together with other tapes, to the northern location.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly in 1996, 1997, when division units were disbanded. We got hold of a large number of tapes at that time. Some installations were closed down and their tapes were taken to the northern location. The whole army was being reorganised and transformed. We were not under any obligation to store these tapes and the material recorded on them. The moment the intelligence section returned them, that meant they -- that they lost their importance. However, there was no time to erase everything. Some things were dubbed, some things remained on the tapes that were in use, and that happened in 1996 and 1997. They were all stored in the northern location.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 65 ter 854.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Yes, I'd forgotten. I would like to offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P291, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness 854, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was it necessary to receive the last one under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The signature at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
