utterances.text: Witness, what you have in front of you now is a document that was -- that is, I should say, dated 19 September 1996, and it concerns the 2nd Corps command, and it records the hand-over of the 2nd Corps intelligence archive materials. And in particular, under item 1, it refers to a number of archive materials, including 3.5-inch diskettes, 5.25-inch diskettes, UHER audiotapes, audio cassette tapes, as well as archives for the 21st Division, I believe, 22nd, 25th Division, and a number of other files. Does this correspond to your recollection of the timing of the reorganisation of the army and, in particular, with respect to the disposition of tapes and other materials concerning your unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This corresponds to the period of reorganisation of the army. However, I was not involved in drafting this document. I know people who did this from the intelligence section, because I served at that time as commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does it correspond to the materials that were used by your unit? If you can recall, and if not, that's all right as well.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It corresponds to the material that was at the disposal of our unit and that was in the keeping of the intelligence section. This must have been preceded by a process of gathering the material in our unit and turning it over to our intelligence section, but I didn't get involved personally.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, on the right-hand side, in Serbian, it says that these documents had been seized. The same must read in English. So I don't know what the relation is between this witness and the documents. What can he possibly know about the substance if -- if this is being introduced through him and the documents have been seized, because he says he wasn't involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Vanderpuye did not finish his questioning to this document. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know who Kasim Mesic is? He's indicated as a signatory to this document.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kasim Mesic was chief of the electronic warfare section within the intelligence organ of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did his -- well, did he have any particular relation to the intercept operation that you were attached to?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He was an officer who had graduated from the military academy specialising in counter-electronic warfare, and he had close ties with our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would again offer this into evidence. I think there's a sufficient enough nexus between the witness's work and the signatory to the hand-over of this material. I actually don't see in the English translation that it says "seized" - maybe I just missed it - but it does say that it was handed over. I think that's a sufficient enough basis, but I'm prepared to live with the decision either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber's of the view that we can't see enough reason for a connection between this document and the evidence of this witness, especially when he -- when asking your question on page 47, line 25 and the next lines, "It corresponds to the material that was at the disposal of our unit," and so on. And then it says, "This must have been preceded by a process of gathering the material in our unit," and then he said, "I didn't get involved personally." So that we have not enough reason to receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The request is denied. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Just bear with me for one second, Mr. President. All right. I think you'll be happy to hear that this concludes my direct examination. I appreciate your indulgence. And thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We all have been very patient. It was late enough your finish. You took -- you took much longer than expected and indicated by you. Mr. Tolimir, do you have cross-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do wish to cross-examine the witness, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the witness to make a short pause after my question and to follow the interpretation as recorded on the screens. I will do the same so that we do not overlap. Can we call up 1D128. It's a book which I will use in cross-examining this witness. It is in English. It is a book written by Cees Wiebes about intelligence work in the course of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the period between 1992 and 1995. In order to see the source in the book can we turn to page 5 in e-court and chapter -- or, rather, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says as follows: "This study is an appendix to the Srebrenica report by the Netherlands Institute for War Documentation. A central position in the study is occupied by the role of national and international intelligence and security services in the war in Bosnia in general and Srebrenica in particular." This is my first question for the witness: Did you in any way participate in the development of this study of the Dutch institute? Did you in any way contribute to it?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you the following brief answer: On the order of my superior I gave a statement. I don't know which year that was precisely. There were representatives of NIOD, N-I-O-D, there at the time, and the statement I gave was, in fact, my view of the situation in Srebrenica in terms of electronic reconnaissance. The view that I gave was based on the intelligence gathered by interception. This statement was subsequently published on the internet, though I must say that nobody told me that it would be published subsequently. At that point in time, my superior came to my office and said that I should talk to these people, and, in fact, I could not have talked to them without previous approval from my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you, in fact, if you needed a prior approval from the BH Army to talk to these people, to the ICTY, or any other international organisations. Did you, in addition to this verbal order from your superior, have any written consent allowing you to get involved in these sort of discussions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I think that NIOD was the first group to address these issues. Others followed later. In the case of NIOD, I had a verbal approval from my superior, and he in turn from those higher up, I suppose, for this discussion to take place, because others participated in discussions with them. Before my arrival here, I sought and was given both an order and an approval from the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain for the Trial Chamber what NIOD stands for? Secondly, did you have a written -- did you receive a written approval for your testimony here, since you are now in retirement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: NIOD is a Dutch acronym standing for the Dutch Institute for War Documentation, in former Yugoslavia or in general, I don't know, and I did not need any sort of approval for the testimony that I'm giving right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show up -- show or call up 1D128. This is page 2 -- this is page 45 in the e-court of the book. Let me quote this: "The existence of intercepts can be construed from interviews" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Tolimir, could you please first give a reference where on these two pages is the passage you are quoting, for the sake of the interpreters. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I -- I just want to make sure we're not broadcasting this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 5 from the top. Page 297, line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could that be enlarged and not broadcast. The English page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not be mentioning names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I can read this if I do not reveal the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I quote: "The actual existence of this comment could be construed from interviews with," this witness, I will not say his name, "who performed the duty mentioned herein within the 2nd Corps." So I think we can use it in open session since I did not reveal the identity of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on, please, and put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, this information is in the public domain and it mentions the names of all those who talked to these people including you. You gave statements on issues about which you're testifying here. Did you personally ask for your testimony to be granted protective measures? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President. I object to the question. The question of this witness's protective measures is a matter that I think Mr. Tolimir is aware has -- should be addressed before the Chamber that issued them, and the circumstances under which they are -- they were granted certainly have no bearing in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tolimir, as you are aware, the protective measures were granted by the previous Chamber, not by this Chamber. They are just still in place. Please bear in mind what Mr. Vanderpuye told you and carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: (redacted) And my question was whether he himself sought protective measures for his testimony. If he can answer the question, fine. If not, it is up to the Trial Chamber to give the ruling, but I did not place his identity at risk in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, nobody says that. Mr. Vanderpuye, what is the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I say that, Mr. President, and I say that because Mr. Tolimir has given a page reference of a public document and indicated the witness's name is in it, and given the subject matter of his testimony that precedes this statement, I think it couldn't be more clear who the witness is. So I would ask for that last comment at least to be redacted from the record so that the witness's identity is not put further at risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will redact that portion, but I would like to ask the witness to answer the question of Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I answer, I -- I have to say that this is more of pressure being exerted on me rather than a question. At the time when I performed my work, I had to obey orders, and it's not just me. There were many others who were members of the intelligence department of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we had to abide by certain procedures, including approvals issued by the ministry, by the Supreme Command to me personally. We weren't aware of the workings of the ICTY or of the NIOD. We were told that there were issues we could discuss since these were sensitive matters. As an officer of the army, I was given the possibility to appear as a protected witness, and I accepted the offer. In fact, I wasn't even aware of the possibility for a witness to be not protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise if you feel my question as pressure upon you. This isn't my intention at all. I only wish to look at things that seem logical or illogical. Are you aware of the fact that this publication mentions names and locations from where VRS communications were intercepted? Are you aware of the fact that these pieces of information are published in the book.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must admit that I didn't read these portions of the publication. What I can say, and this wasn't much of a secret, the facilities used for intercepting purposes were formally JNA facilities that were adapted for the new use. It was only logical for these installations, since they remained in the territory controlled by the BH Army, to be used to these ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. These two installations, the northern and southern sites that were used for intercepting purposes, were they under the same command?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You being an officer will understand that in the period up until 1995, after my arrival there, the unit was stationed at three locations that I mentioned. This particular unit was under the direct command of the 2nd Corps command. It was a unit attached to the staff, and you will know what this means. So we were under the command of the individuals mentioned herein. When it comes to their speciality, which was intelligence, they were under the intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you mentioned the intelligence department, does the name of Mustafa Kajrulahovic [phoen], Brigadier General of the BH Army, ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember someone saying at some point that the general died. I don't know anything else about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know which position he held in the BH Army? I'm mentioning him since his name appears in the documents.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that he was on the Main Staff, on the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he have anything to do with intelligence services, since you've just said that the unit was tied to the intelligence service of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that my superiors would be better placed to answer this question. As far as I can remember, he was the head of the intelligence administration for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you send the intelligence you gathered to the intelligence administration of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we sent the information to the encryption service, and I suppose that they forwarded the information to the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who helped you to select and vet personnel who would be involved in intercepting in terms of the suitability of their background to intelligence work?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined the unit in February of 1995. By that time the unit had already been put together. I can't tell you who was behind the selection. I only know that when personnel was looked for they relied on recommendations, and I know that they had to be vetted in a way in the intelligence department, just the same way we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Who did you send the information you gathered at northern and southern sites to in terms of the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sent the information in its original form to the intelligence department of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Am I mistaken in saying that you, in fact, sent the information to the intelligence organ of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you are not mistaken. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the intelligence organ of the 2nd Corps have the obligation to send the information to the intelligence organ of the army?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would only be logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know who was at the head of the intelligence organ of the army whilst you were a member of the corps?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Try as I might, I really cannot remember who was the person number one in that sense in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not a problem. You should give the answer you think you should give. At transcript page 2159, line 22, state that the shifts of operators would be rotated every 24 hours. First of all, tell us if this reflects your memory of the events.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that in 1995 the men rotated every ten days. Now, as for the 24-hour rotation or shifts, we had fixed shifts, but people worked as needed. Whenever the situation permitted, they would rest. Otherwise, they would have to work nonstop, and I did say that operators worked around the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me what was the ability of operators to accurately transmit a conversation, an intercept, if they have to work constantly, 24 hours a day, for a period of ten days?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have in a way answered this question in my statement. Every break, every moment of spare time that there was people used to rest. Of course there was exhaustion, but there was always at the forefront of their mind the idea that either they would be doing this job and enduring it or else go to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday when the Prosecutor showed you documents we saw two documents, one on the left and the other on the right, and one of them said it concerns the 1st Krajina Corps and the other said, "They will go with the 1st Krajina Corps." Is this a serious mistake or is it a reflection of the fatigue experienced by the operator? Did they note down conversations based on how they construed them?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were mistakes, and of course people were tired. And I think this sentence has been taken out of the context. I think it can be quite clearly understood if looked together with the earlier reports and the later reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, but you will admit that if you say it concerns the 1st Corps or they will go with the 1st Corps, the difference is a major one. And this is how it was conveyed in these telegrams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I remind both speakers not to overlap and to wait as that the transcript stopped. Please now your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that it's possible. Mistakes occur, but as I said, this was taken out of context. Information does not only come from people who come by it through electronic reconnaissance. There are other sources too. The information which the ultimately reaches the commander of the 2nd Corps or even higher up would, in fact, have its final form and shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this mean that these intercepts would be read and re-read in order for them to get their final form?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you will know that the information could not be forwarded to the commander in this particular form. We had an electronic warfare department in our unit which had six men, I believe -- seven men, I believe, and all of them read these reports and gave their assessments of them. There was also a department gathering information from other sources. There was also the analysis department, and the analysis department was the last stop for these reports before they reached the commander and before the commanders were briefed on possible activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, do you wish to say that you were part of this chain within the intelligence department, the one that you referred to in your answer?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the security department, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: No, I'm not referring to the security department because it has nothing to do with dispatching and checking telegrams. I wanted to know if you were part of this verification process of intercepts that you referred to a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please set a time-frame on your questions. I don't know if I'm supposed to answer in relation to the period when I performed this specific duty in the unit, or in relation to the period when I was on the intelligence department during the war, or in the intelligence department after the war? Can you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I don't think this question is that important.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have these documents shown side by side, P2692 and P296B.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: P269A and P296B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it P96 or P69?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P269A, P269B. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we can see --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says it concerns Talic's men, on the right; and on the left it says, "They will go with Talic's men." My question is: Do you notice the difference?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the language, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can one mistake change the whole sense of a message?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At the end of all this analysis process, did you finally establish what it was actually? Will they go or does it concern them?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take this conversation in particular, you are taking this question out of context, because it says clearly at the end, "It has all been settled, because the start is tomorrow."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have you preserved the audiotapes so we can check and redress these mistakes that concern serious matters that are the subject of a trial before a court? Were the tapes preserved with intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've seen from the records that most tapes had been turned over to the relevant command. Whether this intercept was one of them on one of the preserved tapes, I cannot say now because I don't know what the section has dubbed onto different tapes and what not. That was not my job. My job was to collect the raw material and pass on this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 2184, lines 21 and 22 of the transcript, you say the following: "I am sure that the entire truck-load of such notebooks had been burnt because we had no firewood." Now, my question is: Is it logical to burn evidence of an activity that you were trying to document as firewood?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, Mr. President, I would respond with a question that doesn't require an answer. Is it logical for there to be a war in the 21st century? Of course it would be logical that the life and the lives of people who were working on this were more important than documents. I allow that mistakes were made, but if it's -- it is logical also that if you have no firewood you will use paper to make a fire. And to add just one more thing. Just before I came to the unit, once a report was typed up it became official. There was no responsibility or accountability for any information written down in hand by any -- on any piece of paper. Yes, there was one truck-load of paper that was burnt, but not all of them were documents. There was all sorts of paper on that truck. There were too many tapes for all of them to preserve -- to be preserved. Even in the former JNA, some tapes were handled, then erased, then returned to operators for further use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Tolimir. We are running out of time. We must have the second break now, and we will resume at 1.00. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I just want to tell you we have to -- you have to stop your cross-examination for today three minutes earlier because I want to raise some procedural matters. Now you have the floor. Please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since we will continue our examination tomorrow, you please interrupt me when it's time, or my advisor will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, at transcript page 2160, line 7, you said that in 1995 your unit numbered some 50 to 60 men. In July 1995, how many people were assigned to the northern and southern locations of those who were on duty, excluding those who were resting at that point?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you precise information. I can tell you that, in general terms, between eight and ten people worked in a single shift in northern and southern locations. In other words, altogether some 15 to 18 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And how many platoons did you have?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we had had two platoons monitoring radio relay communications, one platoon monitoring shortwaves, one radio jamming squad, and the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is this consistent with the number of 50 to 60 men that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly. I think that in the documentation you could find a list. Let's say you had 17 to 18 men per platoon and then some KT platoon would bring it up to 36, and then we had four to five men in the encryption department, and then the command where there was the company commander, deputy, and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In this book --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 1D128, page 299, which is page 46 in e-court, paragraph 2. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, if you speak English and I'm quoting paragraph 2: "The question that now needs to be answered is: What was possible regarding the processing of the intercepts in realtime? Simple arithmetic shows that if the number of channels multiplied by the number of required personnel is greater than the number of available personnel, then near-realtime processing and reporting is impossible." Five lines further down it reads: "If we assume on the basis of this estimate that an absolute minimum of ten channels had to be monitored continuously, that three persons were needed per channel for interception, transcription, and reporting, and that there was a rotation of three shifts a day and a seven-day working week, then at least 90 operators would have had to be active at the northern facility alone, not to mention 15 or 20 staff for support, technology, security, catering, and so on. Hence, if there were 20 channels - probably a more realistic estimate - then at least 180 people would be needed. In reality, a maximum of ten people worked at the northern location. Most of the communication was recorded on tape. It seems, therefore, that near-realtime analysis and processing was unattainable." This was a rather long quotation from the book. I think you were able to follow and that you can answer my question. I would like to hear your comments on this analysis provided by the author of the book. This is a contribution or an attachment to the report on Srebrenica, and it is a very serious study produced by a Dutch authority. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen nor read the study. I've already said what was required in order to have matters as ideally they should be in the army. The author presented the analysis that reflects his view of what seems fit. In my view, this is an unrealistic analysis which does not correspond to the reality that the personnel was faced with at the time. It could have several objectives: To deny or to demonstrate the way matters should be. I took different figures and elements into my analysis, and I know the way people worked, and I'll stop there. Would you believe me when I say that on holidays or at weekends I would serve as many as 25 networks, communications networks? If we proceeded from the number of channels, let's say 12, and then calculate the number of personnel we need, we would not end up with the number of 180 but with the number of 580. What we were able to have was one channel, and the device scanned constantly, hopping from one channel to the other. Whenever an interesting conversation was come across, intercepting would start. If the conversations were not interesting, they would be skipped. Perhaps I will write a book some day. I may be already preparing one. And then based on documentation, we will demonstrate that a job of work can be done with the minimum of forces if one likes what he's doing and if one puts his all into it. I don't see what the point of reading in analysis is. I think that it's a bit futuristic, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me stress again that this is an attachment to the report on Srebrenica by the DutchBat. It is the contribution for the war documentation produced by the Dutch government. There was a trial connected to this issue, and this documentation was submitted for the purposes of this trial. I'm reading this in connection with what you said yesterday, and it is up to the Trial Chamber to compare this with what you were saying. You said that you had between 50 and 60 men. Is it possible for 50 to 60 men to do what the minimum of -- of 180 would be required to do?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that in the course of our work we showed what was possible. We showed that everything was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You and your unit numbering 50 to 60 men, were you able to do what the author of this book claimed was impossible? Can you please answer for Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will say upon response -- full responsibility and under oath, I will give you a short answer and that's yes. If you want a long answer, let me tell you that there were individuals who gave their view and understanding of matters long after the war was over. And I would very much like these people here to do -- to form a shift and see if this can indeed be done by as many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that this analysis was produced on the basis of documentation adduced at trials, including this one?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This will be repetitive. I don't know what they did and how much they did. I only know what the unit I headed in 1995 did and how much it did. It is their right, regardless of their level of professionalism and qualifications, to write what they want.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's why I asked you at the outset if you gave any statements to them and if you communicated with them with the approval of your superiors. They approached this study in a serious manner, going as far as to talk to the people concerned. So did you or did you not co-operate with the authors of this book?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the authors are. What I know for a fact is that I did not discuss this. What we discussed were general matters such as, to the best of my recollection, that Srebrenica had been planned six days earlier, when they were looking for tyres for trucks and buses. Already at that time we alerted the command to the fact that something was going on, not to speak of the fact that the Pribicevac installation was set up at that time, which was the primer. Now, as for this, I don't know how they came by the information and how they ultimately saw the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I didn't want to go into all these various topics, but you've mentioned on several occasions the setting up of this Pribicevac installation, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we were intercepting communications, we came to hear that this was an extension that was 311, this new extension, 311, that was introduced.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown document 1D129, page 2. This is an analysis of the air-lift conducted by the BH Army, and I'm referring to the air-lift with Srebrenica and Zepa, or above Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at page 2, lines 1 through 8. And I will read the relevant portion. It's the line below headline "Introduction." "Between the 27th of February, 1993, and the 7th of May, 1995, there was an air-lift from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to meet the needs of the enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. The main aim of introducing and maintaining the air-lift was to transport and ensure combat equipment, evacuation of wounded, the functioning of government organs in the enclaves, additional training of the officer corps on free territories of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to maintain communication." You see, this was in place as of the 27th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now turn to page 3, lines 3 through 3 [as interpreted]. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Line 3, I'm reading: "The first flight for Srebrenica took place on the 27th February 1993," and so on. This document says that flights for Srebrenica started just after the protected areas was established. Then we have page 7, line 39, 40, and 41. Let us look at (B), "Engagement of forces and equipment." "The air-lift was organised on the 31st December," it says 1995, but that's a mistake, it should be 1994, "and 7th May 1995, with the forces and equipment of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and included the use of helicopters and crews of the air force and anti-aircraft defence of the BH Army." Now, let us look further down. It says: "Hours of flight, 10.25. "Expenditure of fuel, approximately 8.200 litres. "Transported to Zepa: UBS 17 tonnes." That's why this forward command post was set up there starting with February 1995. These activities of the BH Army begin early in 1995. Now, I want to ask you, did the Drina Corps work in parallel to that, in response to that, in setting up this forward command post in the time when this was a protected area?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this document has anything to do with me. I don't know who wrote it. Our job was to provide our opinion as gatherers of intelligence. You just confirmed that this extension line was indeed established there, and a moment ago you discussed an analysis made by some gentlemen saying that we were not able to intercept it, we could not listen to it, et cetera, and I agreed with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This author spoke of the need to process information in realtime. If the Army of Republika Srpska received information in realtime that there were activities preparing to connect the enclaves between themselves and with Tuzla, was it then logical on their part to take steps in realtime to respond to that? This began in early 1995.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a good question, but you can't answer it with a yes or no. First of all, from where I was sitting and the people who were working with me were sitting, nobody every said an attack on Srebrenica is being prepared. We just said something is going on. It could have been anything. It could have been what is referenced here. So you can't say yes or no to your question. We just said something was going on, something was afoot because this radio relay route must have been set up for a reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness page 1 and the last page of this document. This is page 1. Thank you. I'd like the witness to comment. Does he see the heading of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it say "Communication Centre" of the command post of the Main Staff, Kakanj? And the date is 17 February 1996.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a document disclosed to the Defence by the Prosecution. It was prepared by the units to which you belonged. Could this have been sent as a telegram by your unit, because we see it's the -- it's the address of your unit.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have to tell you that I'm seeing this document for the first time, and I have no clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I understand. But this encryption section, does it belong to the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had nothing to do with the communications section. We didn't have any link with them. There was a special section within the 2nd Corps with the communications battalion, signalsmen, and it was their job to organise communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You just said you had nothing to do with the intelligence service, that you had nothing to do with the communications centre, that you had nothing to do with this encryption section. Tell this Trial Chamber to which unit you actually belonged.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You really must have misunderstood me. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: section of the communications centre. They really had nothing to do with us, because we had our own encryption people. The encryptors of the command of the 2nd Corps were in one building, and the encryptors of the intelligence section were in a separate location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we go into private session for just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, would you tell us, your unit in charge of electronic reconnaissance and so on, where did it belong in the general structure, the intelligence department or the staff? Who was your subordinate in the chain of -- your superior in the chain of command, looking from the General Staff down to battalion level?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm answering for the second time. The unit served the purpose of command and control, and it was subordinated to the commander of the 2nd Corps, to whom I had to report every week. Now, along the professional line, and I think you should understand this, the unit was subordinated to the intelligence department. The security department was separate from the intelligence department. The intelligence department prepared orders and other material that the commander would sign. That was one aspect. Another aspect: He sent instructions and reports and analytical documents, et cetera, in order to promote our work. In other words, my unit was directly subordinated to the 2nd Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I understand that, but you said professionally speaking, professionally speaking, you were linked with the intelligence service. I wanted to get that answer earlier, but you probably did not understand my drift. Now, this document that we see on the right-hand side of the screen, and knowing as we know now that you belonged to the intelligence, was this signed by Colonel Edin Hrustic?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that -- is this a document of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it addressed to Enver Hadzihasanovic, Chief of Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, personally?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you read this sentence on the first page: "Pursuant to your oral order, we provide you here with an analysis of the work of the operation of air-lifts to Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde."

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would you confirm that this is an original document, since we received it from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you should ask me that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I request that this document be admitted as a document showing realtime assessment of activities on both sides relating to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have no objection to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: By majority the Chamber is of the view, as earlier this morning, this document can't be admitted into evidence on the same reasons the document earlier this morning tendered by the Prosecution was not admitted into evidence. That means this witness couldn't identify this document, told us that he has seen it for the first time today, doesn't know anything about the content and the author of the document and the authenticity of the document, so that this is not the right person to admit this document into evidence. Although we realise the Prosecution hasn't raised any objection. Carry on, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I requested that this document be admitted as proof of the realistic nature of evaluations. It doesn't matter that the witness doesn't know who wrote it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber has ruled on your request. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just a moment ago, you decided to admit 45 documents that the witness had not seen. Let me now ask for 1D151.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document is not in e-court, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have in e-court 1D129? Sorry, 1D137. Could we see the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All these are weapons received thanks to the air-lift. Quoting line 6 from the bottom: "On 10th February 1995, three prostitutes were found and brought into custody in Zepa who had been in the UNPROFOR base, Russian battalion, for ten days, and as a result of their questioning, it was found that they had told of the entire situation and basic concepts of combat activities. I therefore suggest that you change the route. It could be done from the direction of Zepa towards Kladanj. "To our ultimate victory." Signed, "Naser Oric." What I'm trying to tell you, Witness, is that all sorts of vagabonds and prostitutes knew what was going on in the area, and your main commander asked for the route to be changed. Did you know this, as an officer?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I never questioned these prostitutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have to stop your examination for today. We have only very few minutes left and we will continue with the evidence of this witness tomorrow morning. Just in brief, you have requested in one -- in paragraph 16 of your response to the Prosecution's motion to convert eight proposed 92 bis intercept operator witness to Rule 92 ter witnesses. We have addressed the Chamber with your request to have the possibility to review the original, the diaries, notebooks, and typed intercepts. I would like to ask the Prosecution if there are any concerns, objections, to that request.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon to Your Honours and everyone. I'll just field that one, Mr. President. I actually met with Mr. Gajic last week. We produced for him all of the relevant original notebooks. He had an opportunity to spend some time reviewing them. There were also, I believe, packets of original intercept material, the actual printouts among those notebooks. And as always, should the Defence seek to review any of the originals, we will make them available as we have in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Then I think -- Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can only confirm what my learned friend from the Prosecution just said. A few days ago I had occasion to review a number of these notebooks. I can't remember how many, but around 20, I think. That request we made in our submission has practically been fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. The Chamber is satisfied this problem is solved. The second matter is the following: We received this morning the corrigendum to the Prosecution's supplemental motion for leave to amend the 65 ter exhibit list. Now we have the right document and translation. I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir, would you like to comment this motion of the Prosecution? Is there any problem or objection to this admission of additional two documents to the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We need some time to consult, my legal advisor and I, and perhaps if you allow me we will give you an answer at the beginning of the session tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. We need the answer before the next witness appears here in the courtroom. Thank you very much. And I would like to remind the Prosecution that there is an outstanding matter. In our decision of the 30th of March, 2010, we asked the Registry to mark for identification several documents, and I was told that the Registry asked the Prosecution to provide them with the exhibit -- no, with the 65 ter numbers of these documents. That hasn't been done yet, and we would be very happy if you could do that as soon as possible. These were -- have been my procedural matters for today. We have to adjourn. I apologise that we dealt with these procedural matters in your presence, but it was the most practical way because of your protective measures. We have to adjourn. We resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 2nd day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
